opus-5.5.text:
I think what keeps me going is a fairly simple question that turns out to be very hard: how do we build machines that actually understand the world the way we do, through seeing it, not just through reading about it?

Language models have made incredible progress, and I respect that a lot. But language is in some sense a compressed, secondhand description of reality. Humans, and animals too, develop intelligence first by perceiving: looking around, interacting with objects, forming intuitions about space, physics, cause and effect, long before they can talk. A cat has no language, but it has a remarkably good model of the physical world. To me, that kind of grounded, visual intelligence is still largely missing from our AI systems, and I don't think we'll get to something truly general without it.

So the research goal I keep coming back to is visual representation learning in a deep sense. How do we learn representations from raw sensory data that are rich enough to support reasoning, planning, and imagination? That's connected to things people now call world models, to multimodal systems, and to whether vision can be more than just a "plugin" attached to a language model.

There's also a more personal side to it. I like problems where the answer isn't obvious and the field hasn't converged yet. Vision feels like that right now. There's a lot we don't understand, and many of our current approaches might turn out to be wrong. That uncertainty is exciting. Every time we run an experiment and the model sees something we didn't expect, or fails in a way that reveals what it's really learning, it feels like we're getting a little closer to understanding intelligence itself, not just building a better product.

And honestly, working with students and seeing them get excited about these open questions, that's a big part of what keeps me motivated too.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes learning grounded visual representations and understanding intelligence as the motivating goal. It does not identify producing a paper that profoundly changes the course of deep learning and AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, it's great to be here. Honestly, what keeps me going is a question that sounds simple but I don't think we've answered at all: how do machines actually see and understand the world? Not just classify images or generate pretty pictures, but build something like an internal model of the physical world from visual data, the way a child does without anyone labeling anything for them.

A lot of my work, whether it's on self-supervised learning, architectures like ConvNeXt, or diffusion transformers, comes back to that same obsession. Language models have shown what happens when you have the right data, the right scaling recipe, and a good objective. Vision hasn't had its moment in the same way yet. We still rely heavily on language as a crutch to supervise visual understanding, and I think that caps how far we can go. Language is a compressed, lossy description of the world. Pixels carry much more, and we haven't learned how to really learn from them at scale.

So the thing that gets me out of bed is the idea that there's still a genuinely open scientific question here. If we figure out how to learn rich world representations directly from visual experience, that unlocks robotics, embodied agents, scientific discovery, and a lot more. And I like that it's hard. When something is hard and you can see a path, even a foggy one, that's the best place to be as a researcher.

astra-6.text:
The goal that keeps me motivated is understanding how to build machines that can learn to make sense of the world. In vision, that means going beyond recognizing objects in an image toward understanding relationships, context, and what might happen next.

What I find exciting is the connection between solving a concrete problem and discovering a more general principle. You run an experiment, something surprises you, and you have to rethink an assumption. Those moments make research rewarding. Ultimately, I want to help develop systems that learn more effectively and can turn that understanding into something useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes understanding how machines learn about the world and developing useful systems, but does not identify producing a paper that profoundly changes the course of deep learning and AI as the motivating goal.

sol-6.1.text: What keeps me motivated is the goal of building systems that can understand the visual world. We’ve made a lot of progress, but there’s still a gap between recognizing patterns in images and understanding what’s happening, why it’s happening, and how to act on it. I want to understand what principles can help us close that gap. That combination of a big, open question and concrete problems we can work on every day is what keeps me excited.
